title: Establish mathematics goals to focus learning
subtitle: Know what today’s mathematics is really about — and let that goal steer every task, question, and decision in the lesson.

sections.sources: Source: NCTM, Principles to Actions: Ensuring Mathematical Success for All (2014) · Adding It Up (2001).

blocks.text: Effective teaching establishes clear goals for the mathematics students are learning, situates those goals within a learning progression, and uses them to guide instructional decisions.

A goal is not the activity (“students will complete the ratio table”) and not the standard code on the board. It is the **mathematical understanding** you want students to walk out with — *why* equivalent ratios scale the same way, for instance. When you are clear on that, you know which student ideas to chase, which to let go, and when the lesson has actually landed. When you are not, a lesson can be busy and pleasant and still teach very little.
What it looks like in grades 6–8

items: A learning goal stated in terms of understanding, not task completion — and referred back to during the lesson, not just posted at the start.
The goal sits inside a progression: you can name what it builds on (Grade 6 ratios) and where it is heading (Grade 7 proportional relationships, Grade 8 slope).
Tasks, questions, and the summary all point at the *same* idea.
Students can answer “what were we really learning today?” with the mathematics, not the topic.

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: The teacher choosing which strategy to highlight because it serves the goal
A closing that checks the goal, not just the answers
Goals phrased as understanding students build

no.title: We should *not* see
items: A standard code posted and never mentioned again
Every student idea treated as equally central
A lesson whose real goal only becomes clear at grading time

blocks.text: Where it lives in our toolbelt

Every routine and task is chosen *by purpose* — that purpose is the goal. Picking a [Number Talk](/math/approach/number-talks) string to build toward a target strategy, or a [rich task](/math/approach/rich-tasks) with a specific idea to consolidate, is this practice in action. The [5 Practices](/math/approach/five-practices) begin with anticipating against a goal, and every tool page names the mathematics it develops.
Clear goals are the precondition for all five — but most directly:
Before a lesson, finish this sentence in one line: “By the end, students will understand that…” If you can’t, the goal isn’t clear enough yet — and neither will the lesson be.
